en: The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāḍitarāja, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Nadi of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...

There was a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, along with five hundred bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and immeasurable members of the eight classes of beings—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all surrounding the Buddha before and behind as he preached the Dharma.

At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Siṃhavicitrarāja. He rose from his seat, approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"In the past, I have frequently attended great assemblies in the presence of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of buddhas, yet I have never seen what I see now.
I wish to ask a question; I only pray that you will grant me your permission."
The Buddha said,
"I shall explain it for you according to whatever you ask.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What supreme practices did the Tathāgata cultivate in the past, that he has now attained such a state as the Honored One among gods and humans, surrounded by bodhisattvas, the great assembly of śrāvakas, and the eight classes of beings—devas, nāgas, and so forth—who offer him worship, reverence, respect, and praise?”
"I pray that you will expound upon the causes and conditions of the past, so that all sentient beings may obtain great and wholesome benefit.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
It is because you are now able to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings that you have asked this question.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
I shall explain this for you.

Noble son, I recall that in the past, immeasurable eons ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Acintyaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

At that time, there was an elder named Udgata-dāna (Shangshi) who, relying on his own great wealth and power, did not believe in the True Dharma and harbored no heart of refuge or reverence toward the Buddha.

There was a bhikṣu named Vijaya-sambhava who, seeing this elder, gave rise to a heart of compassion and employed great skillful means, intending to cause this man to resolve to practice and attain perfect enlightenment.
Having formed this thought, he went to the householder’s home.

At that time, Upadāna beheld the bhikṣu, whose countenance was exceptionally sublime and who was fully endowed with majestic virtue; his faculties were tranquil and composed, and his radiance was blazing. Feeling profound reverence, he immediately rose to welcome him.
Having completed his prostrations, he prepared a seat and invited him to sit. Joining his palms, he addressed him, saying:
"Reflecting upon my own meager merit, I am suddenly honored by your gracious visit.
At that time, the bhikṣu said to the householder:
“There is a great Dharma-gate named the Eight Maṇḍalas, whose merit is immeasurable.
I shall now explain it for you, desiring to extensively benefit and bring wisdom to all devas and humans.”
If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, are able to practice it, they will obtain four superior rewards in whatever place they are born:
first, they will be born in the same realm as virtuous friends and great Bodhisattvas, possessing a large retinue and abundant wealth;
second, having many followers, they will enjoy sovereign and unimpeded freedom.
Third, their physical characteristics are perfectly complete and they are free from illness;

fourth, all necessities arrive naturally according to their thoughts, and even if they were crushed by a mountain, their bodies would feel no pain; they are able to know the mental inclinations of sentient beings and, out of compassion and pity, protect and rescue them.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, Upāśikṣa was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated again with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet and praised him, saying:
“Excellent! I pray that you will extensively expound the most supreme Dharma-gate of the eight maṇḍalas, which I shall practice and study.”
The bhikṣu said to him:
"If you wish to know this most supreme Dharma, first make this vow:
'I desire to make offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time, the assembly of great bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.'"
Having spoken these words, one should construct a square altar at the site of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, called a *maṇḍala*.

Its dimensions may vary according to the occasion; its smallest size is four finger-widths or one span (*vitasti*) in length and breadth. One should use various perfumes and other materials, or construct it upon the ground.
Within the square courtyard, eight circular arenas are arranged for the purpose of making offerings to the eight bodhisattvas.
Who are these eight? They are:

Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Maitreya, Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.
Thus it is, householder!

These eight maṇḍala supreme dharma-gates were taught by that inconceivable Tathāgata Prabhāsa; I have personally received and upheld them, and now I shall explain them to you. You should practice and study them, causing them to spread widely.
Dedicate these roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Householder, you should know that if there are those who practice these eight dharmas, they are thereby making offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, the assembly of great Bodhisattvas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas;
such persons are constantly protected by the devas.”
If kings are able to practice and study this themselves, or cause others to do so, all evils within their kingdoms will be extinguished.

Any sons of good family or daughters of good family who are able to practice and study these eight Dharma-gates will, after the end of their lives, not fall into the evil destinies, nor into borderlands, nor into wrong views, nor into unfavorable moral discipline, nor be born into impoverished households.
Therefore, you should know that those who wish to obtain superior rewards in the present and future should study the eight kinds of Dharma-gates mentioned above;

likewise, those who wish to receive a body that is handsome, intelligent, and of sharp wisdom, or who wish to be reborn above in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings, should also practice and study the eight maṇḍalas.

Likewise, those who wish to be born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and even in the abodes of Śakra, Brahmā, Māra, or a Cakravartin King, should all practice and study the eight dharmas mentioned above.

If one wishes to be born into a prominent family among gods or humans, to possess a perfected retinue and overflowing wealth, to have peace and happiness of body and mind with a far-reaching reputation, to have one's commands and instructions accepted with faith by all, and to be the most honored and supreme among all beings, one should cultivate and study the eight dharmas mentioned above.

If one wishes to cultivate and achieve the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, the fruit of an arhat, the path of a pratyekabuddha, entry into the stage of a bodhisattva, and even up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one should in all cases study and practice the dharma-gate of the eight maṇḍala offerings.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāṇṭarāja, saying:
"At that time, was the bhikṣu Vijayaśambhu anyone other than this?"
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is that very person.
The elder Uttara at that time was none other than I, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Since then, throughout many kalpas, I have practiced and made offerings to these eight dharma-gates, fully attaining the merits and benefits described above.
Other sentient beings who follow and practice according to their ability shall likewise all obtain what I have obtained. Good son!

I have practiced the bodhisattva path for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, fulfilling the six perfections to benefit sentient beings and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment; with all my radiance, majestic virtue, and power, I have destroyed the hosts of Māra’s armies.
By whose power is this?
It is entirely due to the merit of making offerings at the eight maṇḍala practice sites.
Therefore, when sentient beings hear the exposition of these eight kinds of Dharma gates as described above, they ought not fail to study them.

Whether with flowers, incense, and lamps; or with food and drink, banners and canopies, robes, and music; by means of praise, prostration, making vows, and repentance—according to one's capacity, all shall receive blessings and protection.

Alternatively, when practicing the six pāramitās, one establishes a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) by using various fragrant waters or by applying perfumes to the ground; whether using water or earth, one constructs a square or circular altar—this is called the dāna-pāramitā.
When practicing offerings, if one’s actions of body, speech, and mind do not afflict sentient beings, this is called the *śīla-pāramitā*.
When practicing offerings, if insects or ants enter the ritual arena and return even after being driven away, to remain patient at that time is called the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.
When practicing offerings, the continuity of the virtuous mind is what is called the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
Offering with a single-minded focus, without mental distraction, is what is called the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.

When performing the ritual actions, the square altars and circular enclosures are perfectly aligned without deviation; one is skillfully able to master the timing for the establishment or abolition of rites—this is precisely what is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
“Good son! In this way, a single dharma manifests according to the mind and is able to fulfill the six pāramitās.
You should extensively explain and teach it to sentient beings for their great benefit, until they attain Buddhahood.”

When this sutra had been spoken, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāḍitarāja (The Lion’s Majestic King)
